“Foundations of Education” EDU 101

Introduction (Topic: 01)

Ideology is the common understanding and believes that people in a group have accepted by
which to live their lives. Here Islamic ideology will be discussed in this course below because
we are Pakistani and many people living here are Muslims.

Islamic Perspective:

“A continuous process that nurtures the natural potentials of human beings from the intellectual,
behavioural, spiritual and physical aspects in an integrated and balanced manner so as to produce
righteous human beings who will bring goodness to this world and hereafter.”

Islamic Philosophers in this perspective:

   -   According to the scholar ‘Abd Halim Hj. Mat Diah’, 1989:

“Islamic education is a process for all under the purposeful guidance of educators who will shape
                           Muslims based on the teachings of Islam.”

   -   According to the scholar ‘Abdul Halim El-Muhammady, 1993’:

“The purpose of education is to produce the righteous individuals who are willing to take on the
responsibility of the caliphs (successors of Prophet Muhammad) entrusted by Allah to lead us to
happiness in this world and in the next.”

Aims of educating people: (Topic: 02)

   -   To inculcate a noble character
   -   To educate the soul to be refined and perfect
   -   To teach students to do good, respectful and noble deeds
   -   To train students to be courteous and be good human beings
   -   To inculcate cleanliness, purity and sincerity as well as noble practices in students.

Areas of Islamic Education: (Topic: 03)

   1. Character Building:

                                                                                                Page 1

                   “Foundations of Education” EDU 101

Character building is the teaching of values and morals. How to lead a good life, treat yourself
and others? Moral education is critical because it helps you to become a better individual, citizen
and a better person in the long run.

   2. Physical Education:

We would like to have healthy and active people who are constructive contributors to the society.
People who are slow, unhealthy and not well are not good contributors to the society. So, if we
want individuals to live a healthy life, they must be physically fit. This encompasses sports,
games, athletics and any other physical activity that people are involved in. What this all teaches
them is sharing and cooperation because many sports are played in teams. Some sports are
played as individuals events but most of them are not and so there is a lot of good learning that
happens here.

   3. Mental Education:

It is the development of the mind and is the basis of education. How does an individual develop
his capacity to think and use his brain? It happens when in education we make the individual be
embedded in creative, natural and analytical thinking and thinking outside the box through
activities that enable the individuals to solve problems, come to decisions, give their opinions
and recommendations, share their ideas etc. only when we force students to think for themselves
then this mental education proves to be meaningful and fruitful.

   4. Life Education:

Education is not a morning to afternoon activity, it happens outside the school and classroom
also. It happens both formally and informally. Learning through other informal experiences such
as gatherings and markets is also essential for young people. If you only limit education to what
happens in a classroom, people will never learn as much because a classroom in its true sense is
an artificial setting.

   5. Social Education:

We cannot live on our own alone. We will not be able to survive because we will not be able to
do all everything for us, we need other people to help us in our life and so that social interaction
is important. Social education teaches us cooperation, sharing, tolerance, listening, not only
thinking about you but others as well. With the virtual world becoming more and more of a
reality today and the world shrinking to a global village scenario, it is more important for the
individuals today to be socially adapt at how to interact with individuals in your own cultural
setting and other cultural settings.

   6. Sex Education:

                                                                                              Page 2

                   “Foundations of Education” EDU 101

This education is not in the sense of love and romance, this is the education of how you will deal
with the individual of opposite gender. When you are with friends who are all girls and all boys,
you behave differently. But when you are in mixed gathering, you behave differently. Sex
education teaches you how to behave in such gatherings with the individual of opposite gender.

   7. Muslim Faith Education:

This really is religious education. We need people to understand what their religion helps them
learn, understand and do. So in the Islamic perspective, it involves the teaching of Quran,
Hadiths, dealing of the Caliphs and other Muslims, philosophers and all that should be taught to
young people.

Islamic Philosophy-1:(Topic: 04)

Islamic Philosophers

   1. IbnuRushd (520-595 Hijrah)
      He put many good and new ideas not only in the field of Philosophy but also in Medicine
      and Islamic Legislation.
   - His great works:
          Kulliyah fit-tibb: 16 volumes in general medicine
          Foundations of Philosophy (MalbadilFalsafah)
   2. Al-Ghazali (1058-1111)
          Produced more than 400 literary works in Theology (Study of Religion),
              Philosophy, Science and Sufism (a mystic tradition within Islam)
   3. His great works:
          Ihya al-Ulum al-Din: a broad field of Islamic Science, Jurisprudence, Logic,
              Sufism

Islamic Philosophy-2:(Topic: 05)

   1. Ibn Khaldun (1332-1406)
   - Major contribution was in the History of Philosophy and Sociology.
   - Wrote about the History of the world.
      His great works:
          Universal History

1. When was the First BPC Report presented to the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan?

 a) 1949

 b) 1951

 c) 1950

 d) 1952

 Correct answer: a) 1949

2. According to the Objectives Resolution, sovereignty belongs to whom?

 a) Parliament

 b) People

 c) Queen

 d) None of Them

 Correct answer: a) Parliament

3. In which city was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly held on August 11, 1947?

 a) Karachi

 b) Quetta

 c) Lahore

 d) Islamabad

 Correct answer: a) Karachi

4. Who moved the Objectives Resolution?

 a) Liaquat Ali Khan

 b) A. K. Fazlul Haq

 c) Muhammad Ali Bogra

 d) Muhammad Ali Jinnah

 Correct answer: a) Liaquat Ali Khan

5. Which BPC Report is also called the Muhammad Ali Bogra Formula?

 a) Third BPC Report

 b) First BPC Report

 c) Second BPC Report

 d) Fourth BPC Report

 Correct answer: c) Second BPC Report

6. Which form of government was adopted under the 1962 Constitution?

 a) Presidential

 b) Parliamentary

 c) Unitary

 d) None of these

 Correct answer: a) Presidential

7. When was the Constitution of 1962 promulgated?

 a) 8 June, 1962

 b) 5 June, 1962

 c) 6 June, 1962

 d) 7 June, 1962

 Correct answer: a) 8 June, 1962

8. Under the 1956 Constitution, the President was to be elected by ________.

 a) National Assembly and Provincial Assemblies

 b) National Assembly and Senate

 c) Prime Minister

 d) Provincial Assemblies

 Correct answer: b) National Assembly and Senate

9. Who withdrew the first Basic Principle Committee's report?

 a) Muhammad Ali Bogra

 b) Khawaja Nazimuddin

 c) Liaquat Ali Khan

 d) Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah

 Correct answer: d) Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah

10. Under the 1956 Constitution, the official name of Pakistan was declared as _________.

  a) Republic of Pakistan

  b) Islamic Republic of Pakistan

  c) Islamic Republic

  d) Pakistan Islamic Republic

  Correct answer: b) Islamic Republic of Pakistan

EDU101 Assignment Fall 2023
By Pin✌️ And Muhammad.
Question?
1. Explain the philosophical foundations of education. According to your point of view,
which type of philosophy is more suitable in our educational context? Give an answer
with a strong rationale.
(10+10)

Answer:-
As an AI language model, I don't have personal opinions or points of view. However, I can
provide an overview of the philosophical foundations of education and discuss different
types of philosophies that are commonly applied in educational contexts.

The philosophical foundations of education refer to the underlying principles and beliefs
that guide educational practices and policies. These philosophies shape the goals,
methods, and values of education. There are several major philosophical perspectives in
education:

1. Idealism: Idealism emphasizes the importance of ideas, values, and the pursuit of
knowledge. It promotes the development of the mind and character through the study of
essential concepts and moral values. Idealism views education as a process of
cultivating intellectual and moral virtues in individuals.

2. Realism: Realism focuses on the objective reality and the acquisition of knowledge
through direct experiences and observation. It emphasizes the importance of practical
skills and preparing students for the realities of the world. Realism sees education as a
means to provide students with practical knowledge and skills to navigate the world
effectively.

3. Pragmatism: Pragmatism emphasizes the practical application of knowledge and
problem-solving skills. It promotes active learning, critical thinking, and the development
of practical skills that can be applied in real-life situations. Pragmatism views education
as a tool for fostering creativity, adaptability, and problem-solving abilities.

4. Constructivism: Constructivism emphasizes the active role of learners in constructing
their own knowledge and understanding. It promotes hands-on learning, collaboration,
and the integration of new information with existing mental frameworks. Constructivism
sees education as a process of facilitating meaningful and authentic learning
experiences.

5. Humanism: Humanism focuses on the development of the whole person, including
their emotional, social, and intellectual dimensions. It values individuality, personal

growth, and the cultivation of positive relationships. Humanism views education as a
means to promote self-actualization, empathy, and the well-being of individuals.

The suitability of a particular philosophical perspective in our educational context
depends on several factors, including cultural values, educational goals, and the needs
of learners. It is important to consider a balanced approach that incorporates elements
from various philosophies to meet the diverse needs of students. A comprehensive
educational philosophy should take into account the holistic development of students,
promote critical thinking and problem-solving skills, foster creativity and adaptability,
and cultivate ethical values and social responsibility.

Ultimately, the choice of philosophy should be guided by a strong rationale that aligns
with the goals and values of the educational institution, the needs of the learners, and the
broader societal context.

﻿EDU101 Fall 2023 Assignment
Question?1.	Explain the philosophical foundations of education. According to your point of view, which type of philosophy is more suitable in our educational context? Give an answer with a strong rationale.
Answer:The philosophical foundations of education refer to the underlying beliefs, theories, and principles that guide educational practices and policies. These foundations provide a framework for understanding the purpose of education, the nature of learning, the role of teachers and students, and the overall goals of the educational system.

There are several major philosophical frameworks that have influenced education throughout history, including idealism, realism, pragmatism, and existentialism. Each of these philosophies offers a different perspective on the nature of knowledge, the role of the learner, and the purpose of education.

Idealism is a philosophical approach that posits that ideas and concepts are the ultimate reality. It emphasizes the importance of intellectual and moral development and views education as a means to access and understand these higher truths. According to idealism, education should focus on cultivating the mind and character of the individual.

Realism, on the other hand, emphasizes the importance of the external world and the acquisition of knowledge through observation and experience. It suggests that education should be focused on providing students with practical skills and knowledge that are applicable to the real world.

Pragmatism takes a more practical and experiential approach to education. It emphasizes the importance of problem-solving, critical thinking, and the application of knowledge in real-life situations. Pragmatists believe that education should be relevant and responsive to the needs of individuals and society.

Existentialism is a philosophy that focuses on the individual’s freedom, autonomy, and personal responsibility. It emphasizes the importance of self-discovery, authenticity, and personal meaning. In education, existentialism suggests that students should be encouraged to explore their own values, beliefs, and purposes in order to develop a sense of identity and meaning.

Considering the educational context, I believe that a pragmatic approach to education is more suitable. Pragmatism recognizes the importance of both theoretical knowledge and practical skills. In our rapidly changing world, where new technologies and knowledge emerge constantly, it is crucial for students to develop critical thinking, problem-solving abilities, and adaptability.

A pragmatic approach to education emphasizes the application of knowledge in real-life situations, helping students develop the skills they need to navigate the complexities of the modern world. It encourages active learning, collaboration, and experimentation. By focusing on relevance and responsiveness, pragmatism ensures that education meets the needs of individuals and society, preparing students for success in their personal and professional lives.

Additionally, pragmatism promotes a learner-centered approach, recognizing the unique needs, interests, and abilities of each student. It encourages educators to tailor their teaching methods and content to match the diverse learning styles and preferences of students.

In summary, a pragmatic philosophy of education is well-suited to our educational context due to its emphasis on practical skills, critical thinking, relevance, and learner-centeredness. It equips students with the necessary tools to succeed in a rapidly changing world while acknowledging their individuality and unique needs.

Foundations of Education (EDU101)                                                            VU

 SOCIOLOGICAL FOUNDATIONS
       OF EDUCATION
Schools as Agents of Change:
 Literacy today is more than simply being able to read, write and being able to do simple
quantitative skills. Today we talk off:

                     Areas to focus to school as agent of change
•Cultural literacy          • Scientific literacy        •Computer literacy
•Technological literacy    •Electronic/media literacy    •Information literacy
If all this literacy has to be taught, it has to come down to the school level. And therefore,
schools have to be agents of change.

•Dealing with diversity.      •Diversity of culture     •Impact of globalization
• Race, class, gender         •How do schools deal with this?
                                        Individual Actions
Individuals can take one of the two types of actions.

determinism In society, the reasons you behave in a particular way is because an external
force makes you do it. For example, you could not pass the red signal; you have to stop because
following the rules of presence of police makes you do it. This is known as “determinism”
(Determined by external forces)

Voluntarism.         You behave in a particular way because that’s the way you know the right
way to behave and this is known as voluntarism. You voluntarily behave in a particular manner
not because an external force is demanding to behave in a particular way.
Sociological perspective recognizes free will within the context of the power of external
circumstances.

                                    Functional Theories:
        stresses the interdependence of the social system, how well the parts are integrated with
        each other.
        Emile Durkheim: education in all societies of critical importance in creating moral
        unity, social cohesion, and harmony . . . moral values are the foundations of society

Functionalists Assume that consensus is the normal state in society and conflict represents a
breakdown of shared values.

    -   Educational reform is to create structures, programs and 21 century curricula that are
        technically advanced, rational, and encourage social unity.

                                   Conflict Theories

__________________________________________________________________________________
                                            _
                         ©Copyright Virtual University of Pakistan               1

Foundations of Education (EDU101)                                                               VU

   -   Social order is based on the ability of dominant groups imposing their will on
       subordinate groups through force, cooptation, and manipulation.
   -   The glue of society is economic, political, cultural, and military power.
   -   Karl Marks is the intellectual founder of conflict theories.
   -   “Cultural capital” passed on by families and schools.
   -    schools pass on social identities that either help or hinder life chances.
                                     Interactional Theories

   -   Primarily critiques and extensions of functional and conflict perspectives
   -   It is exactly what one does not question that is most problematic at a deep level e.g. how
       students are labeled “gifted” or “learning disabled”
   -   Speech patterns reflect social class backgrounds and schools are middle-class
       organizations, disadvantages working class children.

                          Effects of Schooling on Individuals
Schooling should have three effects on individuals
   •Knowledge                 •Attitudes                •Employment
Teacher Behavior inside classroom
A teacher at any given time performs multiple roles; instructor, disciplinarian, bureaucrat,
employer, friend, confident, educator . . . can lead to “role strain”
Student Peer Groups and Alienation:

   -   Four major type of college students: careerists, intellectuals, strivers, unconnected.
   -   Schools are far more than collections of individuals; they develop cultures, traditions, and
       restrains that profoundly influence those in them.
Education and inequality:

The following must be eliminated from the society in order to bring equality:

• Inadequate schools •Tracking      • De facto Segregation    • Gender discrimination

                                 Bernstein’s Theory
   -    In education, he talks of two things; curriculum and pedagogy.
   -   Code refers to a “regulative principle which underlies various message systems, specially
       curriculum and pedagogy.”
   -   Curriculum defines what counts as valid knowledge . . . pedagogy defines what counts as
       valid transmission of knowledge and evaluation defines what counts as valid realization
       of knowledge on the part of the taught.

                                    Labeling Theory
   -   The labeling approach allows for an explanation of what, in fact, is happening within
       schools.
   -   Labeling theory is interested in why people are labeled and who it is that does the labeling.
   -   Deviance is a social judgment imposed by a social audience.
   -   Race and ethnicity are powerful factors in generating teacher expectations.

__________________________________________________________________________________
                                            _
                         ©Copyright Virtual University of Pakistan               2

Foundations of Education (EDU101)                                                               VU

    -   High expectations in elementary grades are stronger for girls than boys.
    -   “If men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences.” Self-Fulfilling
        Prophecy
    -   The teacher expectations are not automatically self-fulfilling.
Processing Social-Educational Priorities

    -   What should be a school priority?
    -   Education for All; child-centered, activity-centered, experience centered.
    -   Focus on Academically Talented Students

SUBJECTIVE PART
                                  EDU101
01: What is Syed Dynasty (1414 - 1451)?

     This reign was categorized by lawlessness and disorder,
     Most time was spent on repressing the revolts and thus art and literature suffered.

During the time of Mubarik Ali, some literary work was done. “Mubarik Shahi” was written during this time.

02: What is the plan for Human rights education?

Human rights education can be defined as education, training and information aiming at building a universal
culture of human rights through the sharing of knowledge, imparting of skills and moulding of attitudes
directed to:

a) The strengthening of respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms

b) The full development of human personality and the sense of its dignity.

c) The promotion of understanding, tolerance, equality and friendship among all nations, indigenous
peoples and racial, national, ethnic, religious and linguistic groups.

d) The building and maintenance of peace.

e) The enabling of all persons to participate effectively in a free and democratic society governed by the
rule of law.

f) The promotion of people-centered sustainable development and social justice

03: What is the examination system according to 1959 education commission?

Examination System for Secondary Education 1959:

1. The examination system of secondary stage is reorganized. Examinations should be held after tenth and
twelfth classes.

2. Examination record of all examinations be kept safe for certain period.

Nimma Malik                                                                                         Page 1

3. Secondary Education Boards be allowed to issue certificates.

4. Private students should have the same syllabus as those of the regular students and they should be
allowed to sit in the examination.

Examination System for Higher Education 1959:

75% marks on the basis of external examination and 25% on internal assessment. On the certificate and
degrees, the marks gained in the internal and external assessment are entered separately.

1. Examination should be organized in such a manner as to assess the ability rather than memory of a
student. For this purpose, objective tests be prepared and introduced.

2. 40% marks as pass marks, 60% second division and 70% for first division.

3. The duration of time for PhD research should be at least two years.

4. The students are allowed to appear as private candidates for further five years.

04: What are the Objectives of 1959?

Objectives for Primary Education 1959:

1. According to the Commission, primary education should enable a student to read and write.

2. To promote a child’s mental, social, moral and physical growth.

3. To create a sense of good citizenship among children.

4. To create a sense of self confidence and curiosity in the child.

5. To create a passion for hard work in the child.

6. To equip the child with information and skill.

7. To create a love for physical work and games.

      vocational education.

06: What is the Target of primary education in1978 policy?
     The target was to open 13,000 primary schools so that by 1992 all children of the country could get
      admission in primary schools. In addition to this, 5000 Masjid schools were to be opened so that
      children can get religious education along with primary education.
     A target of opening 1,000 workshop schools was also fixed. The aim was to teach children different
      domestic handicrafts and skills so that they might become useful members of the society.

-   When a journey towards inclusive education was ready to take off the federal government developed
    the education ministry to provincial governments.
-   The provincial governments are not conceptually very clear what to do next.
-   At provincial level, the movement of inclusive education seems losing its momentum because of two
    barriers:

1. Attitudes of ordinary school teachers

2. Attitudes of special education teachers

Pre-literate societies are societies and communities that existed before writing began. So, obviously the
means by which information or stories were transmitted was oral. People communicated through oral
language from one generation to the next and that’s how information got moved.

    Question 1:

    Question 2:
    What is the perspective of functional theories and conflict theories?
  : 128 – Sociological Foundations of Education: Theoretical Perspectives
-     Functional Theories: stresses the interdependence of the social system, how
  well the parts are integrated with each other.
-     Emile Durkheim: education in all societies of critical importance in creating
  moral unity, social cohesion, and harmony . . . moral values are the foundations of
  society

    Topic: 129 - Functionalists
-       Assume that consensus is the normal state in society and conflict represents a
    breakdown of shared values.
-       Educational reform is to create structures, programs and curricula that are
    technically advanced, rational, and encourage social unity.
    Topic: 130 – Conflict Theories-1
-       Social order is based on the ability of dominant groups imposing their will on
    subordinate groups through force, cooptation, and manipulation.
-       The glue of society is economic, political, cultural, and military power.
-       Ideologies legitimate inequality and unequal distribution of goods as inevitable
    outcome of biology or history.
-       Whereas functionalists emphasize cohesion, conflict theorists, emphasize
    struggle in explaining social order.
-       Karl Marks is the intellectual founder of conflict theories.
    Topic: 131 - Conflict Theories-2
-       The “Achievement Ideology” of schools disguises the real power struggle
    which correspond to the power struggles of the large society.
-       Educational expansion best explained by status group struggle . . . educational
    credentials such as college diplomas primarily status symbols rather than indicators

    of actual achievement to secure more advantageous places in employment and
    social structure.
    “Cultural capital” passed on by families and schools . . . schools pass on social
    identities that either help or hinder life chances
  Question 3:
  What were the goals of education in Arabic society?
  Educational Goals:
-    Cultivate religious commitment to Islamic beliefs,
  Expertise in mathematics, medicine and science
  Question 4:
  Why the examination system of national education policy was highlighted as
  unsatisfactory?
-    The existing system of examination has been thought in the report as
  unsatisfactory because it does not measure the ability of students.
-    It therefore needs to be reformed and restructured.

    Question 5:
    What facilities were provided to the primary teachers in national education policy
    1998?
-       Existing facilities to be availed fully and new facilities to be provided.
-       Media to be fully used for promotion of elementary education.
-       Uprooting all types of social injustice, work will be done for equal chances of
    education for all.
-       Promoting the elementary education, through formal and informal resources
    will be done.
-       Terms and conditions of service for teachers will be made better and
    employment of teacher will be on merit basis; it will be tried to appoint teachers
    near their residences as much as possible.
-       Poor students will be provided books and notebooks free of cost at the
    beginning of the educational year.
-       In the elementary classes, slates and wooden planks will be introduced again.
-        Subjects like cleanliness of atmosphere, use of computer, population planning,
    moral values and basic health will be included in the curriculum.

  Question 6:
  On which fields the Ibn Rashid provided new ideas?
  He put many good and new ideas not only in the field of Philosophy but also in
  Medicine and Islamic Legislation.
-    His great works:

•       Kulliyah fit-tibb: 16 volumes in general medicine
•       Foundations of Philosophy (Malbadil Falsafah)

     Question 7:
     What effects does schooling on the individuals?
     Schooling should have three effects on individuals
-        Knowledge
-        Attitudes
-        Employment
     Education and mobility, the “civil religion” . . . education amount vs. route . . . for
     the middle class, education may be linked to mobility but or the rich and the poor,
     it may have very little to do with it.
     Inside the Schools:
-        Schools from an organization point of view . . . effects of school size.
-        Curriculum expresses culture.
-        Tracking in public schools, rarely in private schools.

     Question 8:
     What were the goals of the education who were the students and which teaching
     methods were used in the Egyptian period?
     Educational Goals:
-        To prepare priest according to scribe for the empire
     Students:
     Males of upper class
     Instructional Methods:
-        Memorization and copying texts
     Curriculum:
-        Religious or Technical texts
     Agents:
-        Priest and scribes
     Influence on education:
-        Restriction on educational controls to priest elites

     Question 9:
     What facilities were highlighted in the national commission 1959 to be provided to
     the primary teachers?
1.     Teachers of Primary Education should be provided some professional training.
2.     Refresher courses be arranged now and then for the teachers.
3.     The service condition of teachers be made better.

4.     Rewards in cash or certificates be given to teachers showing better working.
5.     For the first three classes of primary education, female teachers be preferred to
     male teachers.
     Residence arrangement for female teachers be made
     Question 10:
     Why is necessary to eliminate the gender discrimination in education?

     Write five characteristics and beliefs of humanistic approach?

Edu101 GDG 2023
Questions :-
Disscuus briefly three laws of learning presented by Edward Thorndike?

Solution:-

Edward Thorndike, a prominent psychologist, proposed three laws of learning that are fundamental
to understanding the process of learning. These laws are known as the laws of effect, readiness, and
exercise. Let's briefly discuss each of these laws:

Law of Effect: The law of effect states that the consequences of an action determine the likelihood
of that action being repeated in the future. Thorndike conducted experiments with animals in puzzle
boxes and observed that behaviors leading to satisfying outcomes or rewards are more likely to be
repeated, while behaviors leading to discomfort or punishment are less likely to be repeated. This
law emphasizes the role of reinforcement and punishment in shaping behavior.

Law of Readiness: The law of readiness emphasizes the importance of an individual's readiness or
preparedness to learn. According to this law, learning is most effective when the learner is mentally
and physically ready to engage in the learning process. Thorndike believed that learners are more
receptive to new information and skills when they have a level of motivation and preparedness to
acquire the knowledge or perform the task at hand.

Law of Exercise: The law of exercise suggests that connections between a stimulus and response
are strengthened through practice or repetition. Thorndike argued that the more frequently a
stimulus and response occur together, the stronger the association becomes. This law highlights
the significance of repetition and practice in reinforcing and consolidating learning.

Overall, these three laws of learning proposed by Edward Thorndike provide insights into the factors
that influence learning and behavior. They emphasize the importance of consequences, readiness,
and repetition in shaping and strengthening learning processes.

                                    Glossary

 Axiology
Axiology is the philosophical study of "values"
 Curriculum
The term curriculum refers to the lessons and academic content taught in a school or in a specific
course or program.
 Epistemology
The word epistemology is derived from the Greek episteme meaning "knowledge" and logos
meaning "study of". So, Epistemology is the philosophical study of "Knowledge"
 Ontology
Ontology is the philosophical study of the nature of being, becoming, existence, or reality, as well
as the basic categories of being and their relations.
 operant conditioning
Operant conditioning can be described as a process that attempts to modify behavior through the
use of positive and negative reinforcement. Through operant conditioning, an individual makes an
association between a particular behavior and a consequence
 Perennialist
Perennialists believe that the focus of education should be the ideas that have lasted over centuries.
They believe the ideas are as relevant and meaningful today as when they were written.
 postmodernization
Postmodernism means literally ‘after the modern era’. The modern era stresses the renaissance
period to the end of about World wars I & II which is from the 18th to the mid or late 20th century.
The modern era was far more predictable the postmodern era. The postmodern era has more risks
and cannot be predicted.

Areas of Islamic Education: (Topic: 03)

Character Building:
Character building is the teaching of values and morals. How to lead a good life, treat yourself and others? Moral education is critical because it helps you to become a better individual, citizen and a better person in the long run.
Physical Education:
We would like to have healthy and active people who are constructive contributors to the society. People who are slow, unhealthy and not well are not good contributors to the society. So, if we want individuals to live a healthy life, they must be physically fit. This encompasses sports, games, athletics and any other physical activity that people are involved in. What this all teaches them is sharing and cooperation because many sports are played in teams. Some sports are played as individuals events but most of them are not and so there is a lot of good learning that happens here.
Mental Education:
It is the development of the mind and is the basis of education. How does an individual develop his capacity to think and use his brain? It happens when in education we make the individual be embedded in creative, natural and analytical thinking and thinking outside the box through activities that enable the individuals to solve problems, come to decisions, give their opinions and recommendations, share their ideas etc. only when we force students to think for themselves then this mental education proves to be meaningful and fruitful.

Education is not a morning to afternoon activity, it happens outside the school and classroom also. It happens both formally and informally. Learning through other informal experiences such as gatherings and markets is also essential for young people. If you only limit education to what happens in a classroom, people will never learn as much because a classroom in its true sense is an artificial setting.

We cannot live on our own alone. We will not be able to survive because we will not be able to do all everything for us, we need other people to help us in our life and so that social interaction is important. Social education teaches us cooperation, sharing, tolerance, listening, not only thinking about you but others as well. This education is not in the sense of love and romance, this is the education of how you will deal with the individual of opposite gender. When you are with friends who are all girls and all boys, you behave differently. But when you are in mixed gathering, you behave differently. Sex education teaches you how to behave in such gatherings with the individual of opposite gender.

This really is religious education. We need people to understand what their religion helps them learn, understand and do. So in the Islamic perspective, it involves the teaching of Quran, Hadiths, dealing of the Caliphs and other Muslims, philosophers and all that should be taught to young people.

His great works:
Ihya al-Ulum al-Din: a broad field of Islamic Science, Jurisprudence, Logic, Sufism
Islamic Philosophy-2: (Topic: 05)
Ibn Khaldun (1332-1406)
Major contribution was in the History of Philosophy and Sociology.
Wrote about the History of the world.
His great works:
Universal History
Summary of the result (religion)
Al-Frabi (870-950 AD)
Major contribution was in philosophy, Logic and Sociology
His great works:
Kitab al-ihsa al ulum: explains the classification and principles of basic science.
Kitab al-Musiqa: a book on music
Information or Knowledge or Much More…..
Our condition: “we are drowning in information and starving for knowledge.”
Hikmah is an abundant and huge gift of Allah. It shows us how to use the knowledge.

Ontological Concepts
The only ontological reality is God himself.
God is external and the universe and man’s existence is a reality but it is an apparent reality.

Foundations of Education (EDU101)

                                                                                          Lesson 01
              INTRODUCTION TO FOUNDATIONS OF EDUCATION
Topic: 01 – Introduction:
Ideology is the common understanding and believes that people in a group have accepted by
which to live their lives. Here Islamic ideology will be discussed in this course below because we
are Pakistani and many people living here are Muslims.
Islamic Perspective:
“A continuous process that nurtures the natural potentials of human beings from the intellectual,
behavioural, spiritual and physical aspects in an integrated and balanced manner so as to produce
righteous human beings who will bring goodness to this world and hereafter.”
Islamic Philosophers in this perspective:
According to the scholar ‘Abd Halim Hj. Mat Diah’, 1989:
“Islamic education is a process for all under the purposeful guidance of educators who will shape
Muslims based on the teachings of Islam.”
According to the scholar ‘Abdul Halim El-Muhammady, 1993’:
“The purpose of education is to produce the righteous individuals who are willing to take on the
responsibility of the caliphs (successors of Prophet Muhammad) entrusted by Allah to lead us to
happiness in this world and in the next.”
Topic: 02 - Aims of educating people:

   -   To inculcate a noble character
   -   To educate the soul to be refined and perfect
   -   To teach students to do good, respectful and noble deeds
   -   To train students to be courteous and be good human beings
   -   To inculcate cleanliness, purity and sincerity as well as noble practices in students.
Topic: 03 - Areas of Islamic Education:

                                                        1. Character       Building:     Character

EDU101
Conflict Theories (130–131)

   1. Conflict Theories: Emphasize power struggles between dominant and subordinate groups,
      explaining social order through economic, political, and cultural power.
   2. Achievement Ideology: The belief that success is based on merit, often disguising
      systemic inequalities.
   3. Cultural Capital: The knowledge, habits, and social advantages passed through families
      and schools.

Interactional Theories (132)

   4. Interactional Theories: Critique functional and conflict theories by analyzing micro-level
      interactions, like labeling students as "gifted" or "disabled."

Schooling Effects on Individuals (133–134)

   5. Knowledge Impact: The information students acquire through education.
   6. Attitude Development: Changes in student behavior and mindset due to schooling.
   7. Employment Mobility: How education influences career opportunities.

Labeling Theory (137–138)

   8. Labeling: The process of assigning evaluative tags to students, impacting their academic
      and social experiences.
   9. Self-Fulfilling Prophecy: When expectations influence behaviors, reinforcing initial
      assumptions.

Sociological Foundations of Education (123–140)

   10. Functionalism: Focuses on education’s role in promoting social cohesion.
   11. Determinism vs. Voluntarism: Behaviors shaped by external forces versus individual free
       will.
   12. Diversity in Schools: Addressing cultural, gender, and racial differences in education.

Educational Change and Curriculum (140)

   13. Dynamic Education Goals: Adapting aims of education to technological and societal
       changes.
   14. Ideological Curriculum: Balancing worldly knowledge with preparation for the afterlife.

Psychological Foundations of Education (69–121)

   15. Behaviorist Theories: Focus on observable behaviors influenced by reinforcement (e.g.,
       Skinner’s Operant Conditioning).
   16. Cognitive Theories: Emphasize mental processes, like memory and problem-solving (e.g.,
       Piaget’s developmental stages).
   17. Phenomenology: Studies consciousness and subjective experiences, focusing on
       individual perspectives.

Thorndike’s Laws of Learning (74–76)

   18. Law of Readiness: Learning is most effective when individuals are prepared for it.
   19. Law of Exercise: Repetition strengthens learning connections.
   20. Law of Effect: Positive reinforcement strengthens behaviors, while negative outcomes
       weaken them.

Operant Conditioning (83–86)

   21. Positive Reinforcement: Adding stimuli to encourage desired behaviors.
   22. Negative Reinforcement: Removing adverse stimuli to reinforce behavior.
   23. Punishment: Discouraging undesired behaviors through adverse consequences.

Lev Vygotsky’s Theories (109–115)

   24. Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD): The range between what a learner can do
       independently and with assistance.
   25. Scaffolding: Temporary support provided to learners to achieve tasks they couldn’t
       complete alone.

Historical Foundations of Education (141–266)

   26. Pre-Literate Societies: Education focused on survival skills and oral transmission of
       knowledge.
   27. Confucian Principles: Education aimed at preparing elites for governance.
   28. Greek Education: Focused on civic responsibility and personal development.
   29. Roman Education: Prioritized administrative and military skills.
   30. Medieval Education: Centered on religious instruction and social order.

Renaissance and Reformation (149–150)

   31. Humanism: Emphasized classical knowledge, Greek and Latin, focusing on literature, art,
       and philosophy.
   32. Reformation Education: Focused on literacy and religious instruction to build
       commitment to specific religious denominations.
   33. Dual Track System: Differentiated schools based on socioeconomic class and career
       goals.

Important Educational Theorists (151–152)

   34. Confucius: Developed an ethical system emphasizing hierarchy, duties, and societal
       stability.
   35. Socrates: Advocated for self-examination and philosophical dialogue.
   36. Plato: Believed in idealism and classifying humans by intellectual capabilities.
   37. Aristotle: Supported realism and rational observation to guide conduct.

Eastern Philosophers and Islamic Education (153–157)

   38. Farabi: Distinguished teaching from education and emphasized innate human wisdom.
   39. Ibn Sina (Avicenna): Advocated for teaching moral values alongside knowledge.
   40. Biruni: Emphasized the importance of understanding and respecting diverse cultures.
   41. Madrasas: Islamic educational institutions teaching both religious and vocational subjects.

Ottoman Education (157–158)

   42. Madrasa System: Included primary, middle, and high schools, focusing on religious,
       philosophical, and scientific education.
   43. Enderun Schools: Educated talented children for administrative roles, especially from
       non-Muslim families.

Industrialization and Education (159)

   44. Technological Influence: Education evolved to meet the demands of industrialization,
       such as operating machinery.
   45. New Philosophies: Systems like socialism, communism, and capitalism shaped
       educational goals.

Philosophical Foundations of Education (160–163)

   46. Materialism: Focuses on physical and economic realities shaping education.
   47. Existentialism: Emphasizes individual choice and self-directed learning.
   48. Postmodernism: Critiques grand narratives, focusing on pluralism and localized truths.
   49. Critical Theory: Examines how power structures marginalize individuals through
       educational institutions.

Educational Psychology (168–171)

   50. Jean Piaget: Identified four stages of cognitive development (e.g., sensorimotor,
       preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational).
   51. Lev Vygotsky: Emphasized social learning and the role of language in cognitive
       development.

EDU101
Introduction to Foundations of Education

Foundations of Education refer to the fundamental principles and theories that form the basis of
educational practices, policies, and systems. These foundations provide educators and
policymakers with the theoretical and practical insights needed to create, deliver, and evaluate
educational programs. The foundations are interdisciplinary and can be categorized into several
domains:

   1. Philosophical Foundations: Deals with the underlying philosophical ideas that shape
      educational theory and practice.
   2. Psychological Foundations: Focuses on how the mind works in the learning process,
      including cognitive, emotional, and social aspects.
   3. Sociological Foundations: Investigates the role of society in education, including issues
      like culture, class, and social structures.
   4. Historical Foundations: Explores how educational systems and practices have
      developed over time and their impact on current practices.
   5. Political Foundations: Examines the influence of political ideologies and power
      structures on education and educational policy.

Understanding these foundations helps in shaping an education system that is fair, effective, and
responsive to the needs of students and society.

Ideological Foundations of Education

Ideological Foundations of education refer to the set of ideas, values, beliefs, and worldviews
that guide the educational process. These ideologies shape the goals of education, the methods of
teaching, and the expected outcomes. Some key ideologies in education include:

   •   Liberalism: Focuses on individual freedom, equality, and the promotion of critical
       thinking. It encourages education that fosters democratic values and personal autonomy.
   •   Conservatism: Emphasizes tradition, discipline, and social order. It advocates for
       education that preserves cultural and moral values and social structures.
   •   Progressivism: Advocates for an education system that is student-centered, where
       learning is active and experiences are linked to real-world applications.
   •   Socialism: Focuses on education as a means of promoting social equality and addressing
       social injustices. It supports collective decision-making and the redistribution of
       resources in education.
   •   Critical Pedagogy: Encourages students to question societal structures and power
       dynamics, aiming for social change through education.

The ideological foundations of education influence curriculum development, teaching strategies,
and the overall mission of educational institutions.

Philosophical Foundations of Education

Philosophical Foundations of education focus on the theoretical framework of education,
addressing questions about the purpose, methods, and content of education. Philosophy explores
what it means to educate and the values that should guide the education system. It is concerned
with questions like:

   •   What is the purpose of education? Should education primarily aim to promote personal
       development, social integration, or economic productivity?
   •   What is knowledge? How is knowledge acquired and transmitted, and who decides what
       knowledge is valuable?
   •   What are the ethical issues in education? How should educators treat students? What
       rights do students have, and how should educators balance fairness, justice, and equality?
   •   What is the role of the teacher? Should teachers be facilitators, authority figures, or
       subject matter experts?

Prominent philosophical schools of thought include:

   1. Idealism: Believes in the primacy of ideas and the mind, emphasizing the importance of
      intellectual development and the pursuit of truth.
   2. Realism: Focuses on the objective reality and the importance of teaching students about
      the real world using scientific and practical knowledge.
   3. Pragmatism: Advocates for a hands-on, experiential approach to learning, emphasizing
      problem-solving and adaptability in education.
   4. Existentialism: Emphasizes individuality, freedom, and personal choice, encouraging
      students to explore their own identity and purpose in life.
   5. Constructivism: Posits that knowledge is actively constructed by learners as they engage
      with the world, rather than passively received from teachers.

Philosophies of Education

Philosophies of Education represent broader theoretical and practical approaches to teaching
and learning, deeply rooted in specific philosophical traditions. Each philosophy advocates a
different approach to the goals and methods of education.

   1. Perennialism: Believes in the transmission of timeless knowledge, focusing on classical
      texts, critical thinking, and moral development. It stresses that the curriculum should
      reflect enduring human truths.
   2. Essentialism: Advocates for a core curriculum that emphasizes basic skills, knowledge,
      and values necessary for functioning in society. It is teacher-centered and focuses on the
      mastery of subjects like math, science, and history.

   3. Progressivism: Focuses on student-centered learning, emphasizing experiential learning,
      problem-solving, and the development of critical thinking skills. It values creativity,
      inquiry, and preparing students for a democratic society.
   4. Reconstructionism: Seeks to use education as a tool for social change. It emphasizes
      addressing social problems and fostering critical consciousness among students to
      challenge injustice and inequality.
   5. Montessori: Based on the philosophy of Maria Montessori, this approach emphasizes
      hands-on, child-centered learning, where children learn at their own pace and explore
      their interests through structured activities.
   6. Waldorf Education: Founded by Rudolf Steiner, Waldorf education emphasizes
      creativity, imagination, and holistic learning that nurtures emotional, intellectual, and
      spiritual development.

serving as motivational tools across various settings, including education,
workplaces, and parenting. Rewards, such as praise, bonuses, or privileges, aim to
reinforce positive actions by providing desirable outcomes, thereby encouraging
repetition of the behavior. Conversely, punishments, such as penalties, criticism, or

outcomes.

Foundations of Education (EDU101)

       Mental Education: It is the development of the mind and is the basis of education. How
does an individual develop his capacity to think and use his brain? It happens when in education we
make the individual be embedded in creative, natural and analytical thinking and thinking outside the
box through activities that enable the individuals to solve problems, come to decisions, give their
opinions and recommendations, share their ideas etc. only when we force students to think for
themselves then this mental education proves to be meaningful and fruitful.
        Life Education: Education is not a morning to afternoon activity, it happens outside
the school and classroom also. It happens both formally and informally. Learning through other
informal experiences such as gatherings and markets is also essential for young people. If you
only limit education to what happens in a classroom, people will never learn as much because a
classroom in its true sense is an artificial setting.
        Social Education: We cannot live on our own alone. We will not be able to survive
because we will not be able to do all everything for us, we need other people to help us in our
life and so that social interaction is important. Social education teaches us cooperation, sharing,
tolerance, listening, not only thinking about you but others as well. With the virtual world
becoming more and more of a reality today and the world shrinking to a global village scenario,
it is more important for the individuals today to be socially adapt at how to interact with
individuals in your own cultural setting and other cultural settings.
        Sex Education: This education is not in the sense of love and romance, this is the
education of how you will deal with the individual of opposite gender. When you are with friends
who are all girls and all boys, you behave differently. But when you are in mixed gathering, you
behave differently. Sex education teaches you how to behave in such gatherings with the
individual of opposite gender.

    Question 2:
    What is the perspective of functional theories and conflict theories?
    : 128 – Sociological Foundations of Education: Theoretical Perspectives
-    Functional Theories: stresses the interdependence of the social system, how well the parts are
    integrated with each other.
-    Emile Durkheim: education in all societies of critical importance in creating moral unity, social
    cohesion, and harmony . . . moral values are the foundations of society

    Topic: 129 - Functionalists
-    Assume that consensus is the normal state in society and conflict represents a breakdown of
    shared values.
-    Educational reform is to create structures, programs and curricula that are technically advanced,
    rational, and encourage social unity.
    Topic: 130 – Conflict Theories-1
-    Social order is based on the ability of dominant groups imposing their will on subordinate
    groups through force, cooptation, and manipulation.
-    The glue of society is economic, political, cultural, and military power.
-    Ideologies legitimate inequality and unequal distribution of goods as inevitable outcome of
    biology or history.
-    Whereas functionalists emphasize cohesion, conflict theorists, emphasize struggle in explaining
    social order.
-    Karl Marks is the intellectual founder of conflict theories.
    Topic: 131 - Conflict Theories-2
-    The “Achievement Ideology” of schools disguises the real power struggle which correspond to
    the power struggles of the large society.
-    Educational expansion best explained by status group struggle . . . educational credentials such
    as college diplomas primarily status symbols rather than indicators of actual achievement to
    secure more advantageous places in employment and social structure.
    “Cultural capital” passed on by families and schools . . . schools pass on social identities that
    either help or hinder life chances
    Question 3:
    What were the goals of education in Arabic society?

                                                   Hitler

    Educational Goals:
-   Cultivate religious commitment to Islamic beliefs,
    Expertise in mathematics, medicine and science
    Question 4:
    Why the examination system of national education policy was highlighted as unsatisfactory?
    -     The existing system of examination has been thought in the report as unsatisfactory because it
    does not measure the ability of students.

    -     It therefore needs to be reformed and restructured.

    Question 5:
    What facilities were provided to the primary teachers in national education policy 1998?
-    Existing facilities to be availed fully and new facilities to be provided.
-    Media to be fully used for promotion of elementary education.
-    Uprooting all types of social injustice, work will be done for equal chances of education for all.
-    Promoting the elementary education, through formal and informal resources will be done.
-    Terms and conditions of service for teachers will be made better and employment of teacher will
    be on merit basis; it will be tried to appoint teachers near their residences as much as possible.
-    Poor students will be provided books and notebooks free of cost at the beginning of the
    educational year.
-    In the elementary classes, slates and wooden planks will be introduced again.
-     Subjects like cleanliness of atmosphere, use of computer, population planning, moral values
    and basic health will be included in the curriculum.

    Question 6:
    On which fields the Ibn Rashid provided new ideas?
    He put many good and new ideas not only in the field of Philosophy but also in Medicine and
    Islamic Legislation.
-    His great works:
•    Kulliyah fit-tibb: 16 volumes in general medicine
•    Foundations of Philosophy (Malbadil Falsafah)

    Question 7:
    What effects does schooling on the individuals?
    Schooling should have three effects on individuals
-    Knowledge
-    Attitudes
-    Employment
    Education and mobility, the “civil religion” . . . education amount vs. route . . . for the middle
    class, education may be linked to mobility but or the rich and the poor, it may have very little to
    do with it.
    Inside the Schools:
-    Schools from an organization point of view . . . effects of school size.
-    Curriculum expresses culture.

                                                  Hitler

-    Tracking in public schools, rarely in private schools.

     Question 8:
     What were the goals of the education who were the students and which teaching methods were
     used in the Egyptian period?
     Educational Goals:
-     To prepare priest according to scribe for the empire
     Students:
     Males of upper class
     Instructional Methods:
-     Memorization and copying texts
     Curriculum:
-     Religious or Technical texts
     Agents:
-     Priest and scribes
     Influence on education:
-     Restriction on educational controls to priest elites

     Question 9:
     What facilities were highlighted in the national commission 1959 to be provided to the primary
     teachers?
1.   Teachers of Primary Education should be provided some professional training.
2.   Refresher courses be arranged now and then for the teachers.
3.   The service condition of teachers be made better.
4.   Rewards in cash or certificates be given to teachers showing better working.
5.   For the first three classes of primary education, female teachers be preferred to male teachers.
     Residence arrangement for female teachers be made
     Question 10:
     Why is necessary to eliminate the gender discrimination in education?

              INTRODUCTION TO FOUNDATIONS OF EDUCATION
Topic: 01 – Introduction:
Ideology is the common understanding and believes that people in a group have accepted by
which to live their lives. Here Islamic ideology will be discussed in this course below because we
are Pakistani and many people living here are Muslims.
Islamic Perspective:
“A continuous process that nurtures the natural potentials of human beings from the intellectual,
behavioural, spiritual and physical aspects in an integrated and balanced manner so as to produce
righteous human beings who will bring goodness to this world and hereafter.”
Islamic Philosophers in this perspective:
According to the scholar ‘Abd Halim Hj. Mat Diah’, 1989:
“Islamic education is a process for all under the purposeful guidance of educators who will shape
Muslims based on the teachings of Islam.”
According to the scholar ‘Abdul Halim El-Muhammady, 1993’:
“The purpose of education is to produce the righteous individuals who are willing to take on the
responsibility of the caliphs (successors of Prophet Muhammad) entrusted by Allah to lead us to
happiness in this world and in the next.”
Topic: 02 - Aims of educating people:

   -   To inculcate a noble character
   -   To educate the soul to be refined and perfect
   -   To teach students to do good, respectful and noble deeds
   -   To train students to be courteous and be good human beings
   -   To inculcate cleanliness, purity and sincerity as well as noble practices in students.
Topic: 03 - Areas of Islamic Education:
edu101-points-for-mids-pdf:
Islamic Perspective:
“A continuous process that nurtures the natural potentials of human beings from the intellectual,
behavioural, spiritual and physical aspects in an integrated and balanced manner so as to produce
righteous human beings who will bring goodness to this world and hereafter.”
Islamic Philosophy-2:
    1. Ibn Khaldun (1332-1406)
    - Major contribution was in the History of Philosophy and Sociology.
    - Wrote about the History of the world.
       His great works:
           Universal History
           Summary of the result (religion)

    2. Al-Frabi (870-950 AD)
    - Major contribution was in philosophy, Logic and Sociology
       His great works:
           Kitab al-ihsa al ulum: explains the classification and principles of basic science.
           Kitab al-Musiqa: a book on music
There are four areas of philosophical inquiry:

Metaphysics: concerned with questions about the nature of reality. In other words, metaphysics
deals with the real. What is real? Everything that we see, touch, feel, hear, taste is all real.
Everything in this universe is real. So, according to metaphysics, if everything was real then man
should be involved in finding out about everything and that basically is education.
Epistemology: concerned with the nature of knowledge

Axiology: concerned with the nature of values (The moral learning). We want our children to
develop their mind, body, spiritually but we also want them to develop morally.

Ontology is the philosophical study of the nature of being, becoming, existence, or reality, as
well as the basic categories of being and their relations.
Comprehensive education means a complete picture. Allah’s word is the Quran, Hadith,
Fiqa, Teachings of the Prophet (S.A.W) are all Allah’s word and direct studies.
Ayyamilla which is history and culture, tradition, geography will then leads to other Social
Sciences.
Allah’s world which is supporting studies. God created the world and he created it in 7 days.

Allah’s World is science and technology. Allah’s world is made up of matter and energy, and
that is what science teaches wether its plant life, animal life, materials, energy etc . all that is
created by God.

God’s kingdom includes laws and economics. These are given to us that how we do business,
trading or banking. So you can see that education in Islamic perspective is very integrated and all
this together will be you language arts. Because without language you won’t be able to do any of
this.

The Meaning of Philosophical Inquiry
“Whenever people choose to embrace, if their choices are made in a logical, rational manner,
they are engaged in the process of doing philosophy”.
Four specific areas of philosophical inquiry:

   - Metaphysics concerned with questions about the nature of reality.
   - Epistemology concerned with the nature of knowledge.
   - Axiology concerned with the nature of values.
   - Logic concerned with the nature of thinking and reasoning.
Eric Berne’s three important questions:

    Who am I?
    Why am I here?
    Who are all these other people and what do they want of me?
Idealism
Ideas are the only true reality, the only thing worth knowing. Ideas are generated in the hand and
these need to be translated as these are only thoughts. So, as people develop ideas, old ideas lead
to newer ideas, lots of ideas and information is created and that brings us to know how many of
these new ideas do we need.
Focus: Mind
Originators:

     Plato
     Socrates

“Perennialism” Related Educational Philosophy to Idealism
Perennialism
Focus: Teach ideas that are everlasting. Seek enduring realities which are constant, through great
literature, art, philosophy, religion.
Key Proponents
        Robert Hutchins
        Jacque Maritain
        Mortimer Adler
        Allan Bloom
Topic: 26 - Realism
Reality exists independent of the human mind. World of physical object is ultimate reality. They
say that reality is something that exists. The ultimate reality is the physical objects so everything
that you can see, touch and feel is real.
Focus: Body
Originator: Aristotle
Essentialism

Related Educational Philosophy to Realism
Focus: Teach the common core, “the basics” of information and skills (cultural heritage) neede
for citizenship. (Curriculum can change slowly)
Key Proponents

        William Bagley
        Arthur Bestor
        E.D. Hirsch
        Chester Finn
        Diane Ravitch
        Theodore Sizer
Topic: 32 - Pragmatism
Universe is dynamic and evolving. Purpose of thought is action. Truth is relative. The key term
here is evolving which means that when you evolve you change. So, when you change, nothing
can be permanent. Things change, nothing is permanent is the pragmatism approach.
Focus: Experience
Originators

        Pierce
        Dewey
Progressivism
Related Educational Philosophy to Pragmatism
Focus: ideas should be tested by active experimentation. Learning rooted in questions of
learners in interaction with others. Experience3 and student centered.
Key Proponents

    John Dewey
    William Kilpatrick
Reconstructionism Critical pedagogy: Analysis of world events, controversial issues and
diversity to provide vision for better world and social change.
Focus: Freedom
Originators

    George Counts
    J. Habermas
    Ivan Illich
    Henry Giroux
Related Educational Philosophy to Reconstructionism:
Existentialism:
Focus:

      -    Reality is subjective, within the individual. Individual rather than external standards.
  Key Proponents:

      -    Sartre
      -    Kierkegaard
  Topic: 44 - Eclecticism:

      -    There is a way of dealing with all the various models.
      -    Eclecticism is not a philosophical system or model, but rather is the synthesizing and
           personal interpretation of various models to draw out the best components for you.
      -    Thus, you pull the best from various models in an effort to build your own statement of
           personal philosophy.

Edu101 Short notes
Final term
 Challenges in Education System
Challenge No 1 – Low level of literacy
it is currently 51.6% (male 63.7% and female 39.25)
Challenge no 2 - Access to basic education Gross enrolment in primary schools is 855.Some major factors for low enrolment are:
· Poverty
· Long distance from school
• Poor physical infrastructure
• Functional problems
• Not related to market demands
Challenge no 3
Schools curriculum is static, inert and non-responsive to the socio-economic needs both nationally and internally:
Challenge no 4
To evolve an integrated system of national education by bringing Deeni madras and modern schools closer to mainstream especially in curriculum and the scheme of studies.
Challenge no 5 – Financial constrains
Challenges no 6 - Public private partnership
Challenge no 7
Rampant un-employment among the educated youth

Need for strong management information system (MIS)

Inclusive Education :-
The dream of 100% enrolment as perceived in the UN Millennium Development Goals can not come true without addressing the educational needs of children with disabilities.
- Special schools, inspite of all their benefits, have failed to nurture a natural growth of these children because of social segregation.
- The cost of special education is Rs. 30,000 per child per year as compared to Rs. 2500 for a child studying in an ordinary school.
- The most economical solution will be to make the primary school functioning at the doorstep open to all children through inclusive education.
At provincial level, the movement of inclusive education seems losing its momentum because of two barriers:
· Attitudes of ordinary school teachers
it will be difficult to create a welcoming environment for children with special needs
The inclusion of special children will further deteriorate the quality of instruction and the school may collapse.
· Attitudes of special education teachers
They argue that special needs children require a type of “clinical care
The students of public schools will not accept them
They fear that in case the inclusive education is successfully implemented in Pakistan, they will be out of jobs.
Disability Leads to Poverty
Disability leads to poverty in the following ways:
- Loss of income
- Additional cost of disability management
- Exclusion from services
- Low expectations in terms of capacity to learn
- Lack of technical and financial support
- Disabling environment
- Reduced opportunities for work
- Unfriendly job market
Poverty leads to Disability :-
- Overburden
- Poor nutrition
- Illiteracy and lack of awareness about health
- Lack of access to basic services that prevent disability
- Poor health
- Over-working
- risky physical labor environments
- Un-employment
What are accommodations?
Accommodation are changes in teaching methods.
It can include changes in:
- When you teach
- Who teaches
- How you teach
- How the student can respond
- Materials you use
Room Accommodations
- titled desk top
- Special chairs
- Sitting close to the blackboard
- additional lightening
- Stand instead of sitting,
- Picture schedules, visual cues or visual timer
- Color coding
- Have at least part of the room bare with nothing on walls, ceilings or floor.
- Keeping materials
- Divide the class
- Set up lessons
- Change the learning goals
- Create alternative activities
Teacher accommodators
- Do not wear cologne
- Do not wear a lot of jewellery
- Count to 10 before letting anyone answer questions (processing time)
“Pull out” means removing the student from class for a small group of 1-to-1 instruction
Special education
 Individualized supports that give kids with disabilities the extra help they need to learn from general curriculum.
Inclusive education
- Physical therapy
- Curriculum adaptation
- Communication board
- Behavior plan
- Environmental accommodation
Trends and Challenges in Education
Inclusive education
When every child is welcomed and valued regardless of ability or disability.
Role and status of different languages in Pakistan
1. The National Language of Pakistan is Urdu and arrangements shall be made for its being used for official and other purposes within fifteen years from the commencing day.
2. the English language may be used for official purpose until arrangements are made for its replacement by Urdu.
3. Without prejudice to the status of the National Language, a Provincial Assembly may by law prescribe measures for the teaching, promotion and the use of a provincial language in addition to the national language.
4. Urdu- National Language and lingua Franca (MT for only 7%)
5. Regional languages – used mainly in informal social interactions.
Environmental Education – 1
Tbilisi Conference, USSR, 1977
First major conference on the theme of Environmental Education where the following objectives were proposed:
- To create environmental awareness
- To disseminate knowledge and skills
- To initiate new behavioral approaches, at the individual or group levels, towards environment.
- To develop inter-disciplinary view of environment as a dynamic system and to emphasis its complexity
- To help in promotion of environmentally sound development-program towards sustainable growth.
- To create an atmosphere of national, international understanding and global cooperation in areas of environmental priority.
Environmental Education – 2
Educational Objectives
- Bringing about positive attitudinal and behavioral changes in teachers and students, in respect of environmental problems
- creating awareness about past, current and expected situations of environment
- disseminating information and exchanging knowledge
- encouraging and developing critical thinking among students in dealing with real-world environmental challenge
Mainstreaming Human Rights
- Right to fresh air
- Right to safe drinking water and sanitation

Answer:
Realism Curriculum (Topic: 30)

    Attention is given to didactic and object studies in education (use of pictures, TV, videos
         in educational process)

Question #5 :
How can Robert Gagne’s define theory of learning? Marks 3
Answer:        topic#88

Based upon his analysis of research, he believed that the set of variables
influencing the learning of tasks in one domain may not influence the
learning of tasks in other domains. One may generalize research findings to
other tasks within that domain, but not to tasks in other domains.

Thus, factors found to influence the learning of one piece of information
(e.g., overlearning positively affects the learning of telephone numbers) may
be applied to other tasks in that domain (e.g., the learning of names), but
not to the tasks in other domains (e.g., the learning of a new concept).
